questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer maps sensory, short-term, and long-term memory stores.

options.text: Memory has sensory, short-term, and long-term stages
Memory has only one permanent stage
Memory has only sensory and long-term stages
Memory stages are identical in duration

questions.explanation: Memory includes sensory, short-term, and long-term stages with different durations. A single stage or identical durations misrepresent the model.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection shows a flash of light lingering briefly in vision.

options.text: Iconic memory lasts about half a second

questions.explanation: Iconic (visual) sensory memory lasts about 0.5 seconds. Longer or permanent durations describe other stores.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer notes short-term memory holds about seven items.

options.text: Short-term capacity is exactly one item
Short-term capacity is about 7 plus or minus 2 items

questions.explanation: Short-term memory capacity is about 7 plus or minus 2 items. Unlimited or extreme values misrepresent it.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection labels the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad.
questions.explanation: The phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad are working memory components. They are not long-term stores, sensory registers, or reflexes.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer separates getting information in from getting it out.

options.text: Encoding and retrieval are the same process
Encoding inputs information; retrieval outputs it
Storage is the same as encoding

questions.explanation: Encoding puts information in; retrieval gets it out. They are distinct processes, and storage maintains information.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection contrasts shallow and deep processing of words.
questions.explanation: Deeper semantic processing yields better retention than shallow processing. Depth does matter.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A student links new material to existing knowledge.

options.text: Elaborative rehearsal connects new to existing knowledge

questions.explanation: Elaborative rehearsal connects new information to existing knowledge. Verbatim repetition describes maintenance rehearsal.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer repeats a phone number to keep it in mind.

options.text: Maintenance rehearsal repeats information to hold it briefly
Maintenance rehearsal transfers directly to long-term

questions.explanation: Maintenance rehearsal repeats information to keep it in short-term memory. It does not deeply analyze or guarantee long-term transfer.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection contrasts conscious recall with skill memory.

options.text: Explicit memory is only motor skills
Explicit memory is conscious; implicit is unconscious

questions.explanation: Explicit memory involves conscious recall; implicit memory operates unconsciously. They differ in awareness.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer studies in the same room as the test.

options.text: Matching encoding and retrieval contexts aids recall

questions.explanation: Matching encoding and retrieval contexts improves recall. Context can help rather than hurt.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection contrasts external context with internal state cues.

options.text: Context and state dependence are identical
Context dependence uses external cues; state dependence uses internal cues

questions.explanation: Context dependence relies on external environmental cues; state dependence relies on internal physiological or mood cues. They are distinct.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer recalls the first and last items of a list best.

options.text: Middle items are always best recalled
Primacy and recency effects improve recall of ends

questions.explanation: Primacy and recency effects boost recall of first and last items. Middle items are recalled less well.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection contrasts old memories disrupting new learning versus new disrupting old.

options.text: Proactive is old disrupting new; retroactive is new disrupting old

questions.explanation: Proactive interference is old information disrupting new learning; retroactive is new information disrupting old memory. Both involve disruption.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer plots rapid initial forgetting that slows over time.

options.text: The forgetting curve shows rapid early loss then plateau

questions.explanation: The forgetting curve shows rapid early loss that slows over time. It is neither linear, absent, nor total.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer experiences a word on the tip of the tongue.

options.text: Tip-of-the-tongue means the word was never learned
Tip-of-the-tongue means the word is forgotten permanently
Tip-of-the-tongue is retrieval failure with partial access

questions.explanation: Tip-of-the-tongue is retrieval failure with partial access to the target. The word is stored but not fully retrieved.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection suggests painful memories may be pushed from awareness.

options.text: Motivated forgetting is the same as decay
Motivated forgetting proposes unconscious suppression of memories

questions.explanation: Motivated forgetting proposes unconscious suppression of threatening memories. It is not deliberate deletion, absent, or simple decay.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A witness's memory changes after hearing misleading questions.

options.text: The misinformation effect alters memory with post-event information

questions.explanation: The misinformation effect occurs when post-event information alters memory. It does not improve accuracy or affect only perception.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer remembers a fact but not where it came from.

options.text: Source amnesia is perfect recall of origin
Source amnesia is forgetting all content
Source amnesia is remembering content but forgetting origin
Source amnesia is a motor problem

questions.explanation: Source amnesia is remembering content while forgetting its origin. It is not total forgetting or motor-related.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection contrasts memory loss for past events versus new learning.

options.text: Retrograde loses past memories; anterograde loses new learning

questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia affects past memories; anterograde affects new learning. They are distinct.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A student tests themselves instead of rereading notes.

options.text: Testing enhances retention more than rereading
Testing has no effect on retention

questions.explanation: The testing effect shows retrieval practice enhances retention more than rereading. It benefits long-term retention.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that attention moves sensory data into short-term memory.

answer.exemplar: Attention gates transfer from sensory to short-term memory, so unattended sensory information decays before reaching short-term storage.

questions.explanation: Attention is required to transfer sensory data to short-term memory. Unattended information decays.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that echoic memory briefly holds auditory input.

answer.exemplar: Echoic memory preserves auditory input for a few seconds, allowing speech comprehension across brief gaps in sound.

questions.explanation: Echoic memory briefly holds auditory input. This persistence aids speech comprehension.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer chunks digits into meaningful groups to expand capacity.

answer.exemplar: Chunking groups items into meaningful units, effectively increasing short-term capacity without changing the underlying item limit.

questions.explanation: Chunking groups items into units, expanding effective capacity. The underlying limit stays the same.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons about the central executive coordinating subsystems.

answer.exemplar: The central executive directs attention and coordinates the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad without storing information itself.

questions.explanation: The central executive coordinates subsystems and attention. It does not store information.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that retrieval cues reactivate encoded traces.

answer.exemplar: Retrieval cues reactivate encoded memory traces, so better cues improve access to stored information.

questions.explanation: Cues reactivate traces, improving access. Poor cues lead to retrieval failure despite storage.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that semantic encoding outperforms structural encoding.

answer.exemplar: Semantic encoding focuses on meaning, creating richer traces than structural encoding, which only processes surface features.

questions.explanation: Semantic encoding creates richer traces than structural encoding. Meaning beats surface features.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A student reasons that elaboration creates multiple retrieval paths.

answer.exemplar: Elaboration creates multiple retrieval paths by linking new information to diverse existing knowledge, improving later access.

questions.explanation: Elaboration creates multiple retrieval paths. More links improve later access.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that maintenance rehearsal alone rarely yields long-term retention.

answer.exemplar: Maintenance rehearsal keeps information in short-term memory but, without deeper processing, rarely transfers it to long-term storage.

questions.explanation: Maintenance rehearsal sustains short-term memory but rarely transfers to long-term without deeper processing.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that implicit memory supports skill learning without awareness.

answer.exemplar: Implicit memory enables skill learning and performance without conscious awareness, as in riding a bicycle.

questions.explanation: Implicit memory supports skills without awareness. Conscious recall is not required.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that studying in the test room aids recall.

answer.exemplar: Studying in the test room reinstates encoding context, providing retrieval cues that improve recall performance.

questions.explanation: Matching contexts reinstates cues. This improves recall compared to mismatched contexts.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that matching mood at study and test aids recall.

answer.exemplar: State-dependent memory means recall improves when internal state at retrieval matches the state during encoding.

questions.explanation: Matching internal states aids recall. Mood congruence provides retrieval cues.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that primacy reflects long-term storage of early items.

answer.exemplar: Primacy occurs because early items receive more rehearsal and transfer to long-term memory, while later items remain in short-term memory.

questions.explanation: Primacy reflects long-term storage via rehearsal; recency reflects short-term retention.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that spacing study sessions reduces interference.

answer.exemplar: Spacing sessions reduces interference by separating similar material over time, allowing distinct memory traces to form.

questions.explanation: Spacing reduces interference by separating similar material. Distinct traces form over time.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that decay theory attributes forgetting to trace fading.

answer.exemplar: Decay theory proposes memory traces fade over time without rehearsal, though interference also contributes to forgetting.

questions.explanation: Decay theory proposes trace fading over time. Interference also contributes.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that a cue tied to many memories becomes less effective.

answer.exemplar: Cue overload occurs when one cue is linked to many memories, reducing its effectiveness in retrieving any single target.

questions.explanation: Cue overload reduces effectiveness when a cue links to many memories. Specific cues work better.
questions.hint: Too many links weaken a cue.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that evidence for repression remains debated.

answer.exemplar: Evidence for repression is mixed and debated, with some studies showing forgetting of trauma and others showing enhanced memory.

questions.explanation: Evidence for repression is mixed. Some studies show forgetting, others enhanced memory.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that misleading questions can overwrite original memory.

answer.exemplar: Misleading questions can alter or overwrite original memory traces, making eyewitness testimony unreliable.

questions.explanation: Misleading questions alter traces. This undermines eyewitness reliability.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that source monitoring errors produce false memories.

answer.exemplar: Source monitoring errors occur when the origin of a memory is misattributed, producing false memories.

questions.explanation: Misattributed origins produce false memories. Source monitoring is error-prone.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A projection reasons that hippocampal damage impairs new learning more than old memories.

answer.exemplar: Hippocampal damage impairs new learning (anterograde) more than remote memories, which are stored in cortex.

questions.explanation: Hippocampal damage impairs new learning more than remote memories. Old memories are cortical.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A cartographer reasons that spaced practice outperforms massed practice.

answer.exemplar: Spaced practice outperforms massed practice because intervals allow consolidation and reduce interference between sessions.

questions.explanation: Spacing allows consolidation and reduces interference. Massed practice is less effective.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Short-term memory holds 7 items; long-term is effectively unlimited at 1000.
questions.explanation: 1000 divided by 7 equals about 142.86. This ratio illustrates the vast capacity difference.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Iconic memory lasts 0.5 seconds; echoic lasts 3 seconds.
questions.explanation: 3 divided by 0.5 equals 6. Echoic memory lasts six times longer than iconic.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A person chunks 12 digits into 4 groups of 3.
questions.explanation: 12 digits divided into 3-digit groups yields 4 chunks. This fits within capacity limits.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A phonological loop holds 2 seconds of speech at 3 words per second.
questions.explanation: 2 seconds times 3 words per second equals 6 words. This estimates phonological span.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A list of 20 words; 15 are recalled after one hour.
questions.explanation: 15 divided by 20 equals 0.75, or 75% retained. This measures retention rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Shallow recall is 30%; deep recall is 75%.
questions.explanation: 75 minus 30 equals 45 percentage points. This is the deep processing advantage.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Maintenance recall is 40%; elaborative recall is 80%.
questions.explanation: 80 divided by 40 equals 2. Elaborative rehearsal doubles recall here.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Rehearsing 3 seconds per item keeps 5 items for 15 seconds.
questions.explanation: 3 seconds times 5 items equals 15 seconds. This estimates maintenance duration.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: An implicit test shows 60% priming; explicit shows 30% recall.
questions.explanation: 60 divided by 30 equals 2. Implicit priming is twice explicit recall here.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Matched context recall is 80%; mismatched is 50%.
questions.explanation: 80 minus 50 equals 30 percentage points. This is the context match benefit.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Matched state recall is 70%; mismatched is 45%.
questions.explanation: 70 minus 45 equals 25 percentage points. This is the state match benefit.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: First items recalled at 60%; last items at 75%.
questions.explanation: 75 minus 60 equals 15 percentage points. This is the recency advantage over primacy here.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Baseline recall is 80%; with interference it is 55%.
questions.explanation: 80 minus 55 equals 25 percentage points. This is the interference cost.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A list of 50 words; 10 recalled after one day.
questions.explanation: 10 recalled out of 50 means 40 forgotten, or 80% forgotten. This measures forgetting percentage.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Out of 20 TOT states, 12 resolve within a minute.
questions.explanation: 12 divided by 20 equals 0.60, or 60% resolution. This measures retrieval success rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Of 100 trauma words, 35 are recalled after a delay.
questions.explanation: 35 out of 100 equals 35% recalled. This measures retention under motivated forgetting conditions.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Baseline accuracy is 85%; after misinformation it is 55%.
questions.explanation: 85 minus 55 equals 30 percentage points. This is the misinformation impact.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Of 40 facts, 12 have forgotten sources.
questions.explanation: 12 divided by 40 equals 0.30, or 30% source errors. This measures source amnesia rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Remote memories retained at 90%; new learning at 10%.
questions.explanation: 90 divided by 10 equals 8. Remote memory retention is eight times new learning retention here.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Massed recall is 50%; spaced recall is 85%.
questions.explanation: 85 minus 50 equals 35 percentage points. This is the spacing gain.
